summary: Recommends that active queue management be tested, standardized and widely deployed in network devices to improve Internet performance. It also urges continued research into better algorithms. It is a best current practice that updates earlier guidance.

plainLanguage.summary: When too many cars queue at a toll booth, let the system signal drivers early to ease off. This urges routers to do that.

questions: why is red no longer the default aqm
subtitle: Why routers and other network devices should manage their queues actively, and what a good queue-management algorithm should look like.

tldr.problem: Plain tail-drop queues stay full, add delay, let a few flows monopolize the buffer and can synchronize the flows that share a bottleneck. Unresponsive flows threaten the Internet with a new congestion collapse.
tldr.mechanism: Network devices should run active queue management (AQM), dropping or ECN-marking packets before the queue fills, using self-tuning algorithms that do not depend on the transport or application in use.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the recommendations of RFC 2309 and no longer recommends RED or any other specific algorithm by default. It also calls for more research on handling unresponsive flows.

today: RFC 7567 is a Best Current Practice published in July 2015. It obsoletes RFC 2309, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Congestion, Latency and the Update to RFC 2309
sections.content:
Lack of attention to the dynamics of packet forwarding can cause severe service degradation, technically called congestion collapse. It was first observed in the mid 1980s (see RFC 896). Van Jacobson's congestion avoidance mechanisms, now required of TCP implementations, make TCP flows back off during congestion, but the RFC argues that endpoint mechanisms are necessary yet not sufficient: there is a limit to how much control can be accomplished from the edges of the network, so network devices need complementary mechanisms.

Since 1998 low latency has become extremely important for interactive applications. RFC 2309 introduced active queue management (AQM) and recommended Random Early Detection (RED) by default. RED works well with the right parameters, but predicting them proved difficult, so RED has not been enabled by default and its use is limited. This memo keeps recommending AQM but no longer recommends RED or any other specific algorithm by default.

The memo applies to best-effort traffic and to adaptive real-time traffic. It also uses AQM more broadly than RFC 2309 did: any method that lets network devices control the queue length or the mean time a packet spends in a queue. The mechanisms may live in routers, switches and other middleboxes, and in the networking stacks of endpoint devices. It uses the RFC 2119 key words, mostly SHOULD.
sections.plainLanguage: Years ago an older RFC told routers to use one particular early-warning trick. People found that trick hard to set up, so this newer RFC says: keep giving early warnings, but pick methods that set themselves up.

sections.title: The Problem with Tail Drop
sections.content:
The traditional way to manage a queue is tail drop: set a maximum length, accept packets until it is reached, then drop new arrivals until the queue drains. The RFC lists four drawbacks:

  • Full queues. Congestion is signaled only when the queue is full, so queues stay full or almost full for long periods. A burst arriving at a full queue causes several packets from the same flow to be dropped, which can make flows throttle back together (global synchronization) and lower link utilization. Queue limits should reflect the bursts a device must absorb, not the steady-state queue.
  • Lock-out. A single connection or a few flows can monopolize the queue space and starve others.
  • Packet bursts. A large burst can delay other packets and disrupt the control loop, such as the pacing of flows by the TCP ACK clock.
  • Control loop synchronization. Sessions sharing a bottleneck can become synchronized, causing periodic jitter or loss.

Random drop on full and head drop on full avoid lock-out, but neither solves the full-queues problem. The fix for responsive flows is for devices to drop or ECN-mark packets before the queue becomes full, so hosts can react before buffers overflow. That proactive approach is AQM.

For responsive flows, AQM offers four advantages: fewer packets dropped, lower delay for interactive services, no lock-out, and a lower probability of control loop synchronization when the AQM function adds randomness. The RFC stops short of calling this increased fairness, since general fairness among flows requires per-flow state that queue management does not provide.
sections.plainLanguage: A tail-drop queue is like a line that only says "stop sending" once the room is completely full, so everyone waits a long time and some people get pushed out. AQM waves a flag earlier so the line stays short.

sections.title: AQM, Scheduling, ECN and Buffer Size
sections.content:
Queue management and scheduling are related but different. Roughly, queue management algorithms control queue length by marking or dropping packets, while scheduling algorithms decide which packet to send next and mainly allocate bandwidth among flows. The RFC says they are complementary, not replacements for each other. Even devices that use per-flow or per-class queues (Fair Queueing, Weighted Fair Queueing, Deficit Round Robin and similar) need AQM, because scheduling alone does not control overall or individual queue sizes.

An AQM method may use Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) to mark packets instead of dropping them under mild or moderate congestion. That lets a device signal congestion before a transport suffers loss or extra queueing delay.

The RFC also separates buffer size from AQM parameters. The optimum buffer size depends on operational requirements and should generally be enough for the largest normal burst expected. AQM frees a designer from limiting buffer space to get acceptable performance, because it keeps the average queue depth small and reduces the chance that competing sessions block each other.
sections.plainLanguage: Scheduling decides who goes next in line, and AQM decides when to tell people to slow down. You want both. The size of the waiting room is a separate choice from the rule for when to wave the warning flag.

sections.title: Aggressive Flows and the Need for Research
sections.content:
The equitable sharing of a congested link depends on all flows running compatible congestion avoidance algorithms. The RFC calls a flow TCP-friendly when its congestion response approximates the average response expected of a TCP flow. It groups flows into three classes: TCP-friendly flows, non-responsive flows that do not slow down when congestion occurs, and flows that are responsive but less so than TCP.

UDP provides no mechanism to prevent congestion collapse, and streaming voice and video are given as examples that use it. Some applications could even increase traffic in response to congestion, for example by adding forward error correction when loss is experienced. Less-responsive-than-TCP flows may come from poor implementations, a deliberately more aggressive "faster TCP", adaptive video that responds incompletely or too slowly, tunneled aggregates, or applications that open multiple connections or many short TCP flows.

The RFC says there is currently no consensus solution to controlling the congestion caused by such flows, and there is little measurement evidence about how fast these threats are materializing. Even the granularity of a "flow" (a transport flow, a DSCP, a host pair, a subscriber or site) is largely a policy question for the wider IETF community.

Section 4.7 reiterates the call of RFC 2309 for continuing research. Examples it lists include new AQM and scheduling algorithms, delay-based methods, ECN marking that needs no tuning, deployment experience with ECN alongside AQM, tools for deploying and measuring AQM, and ways to mitigate non-conformant and malicious flows. It names data-center incast (many-to-one traffic patterns) as an obvious example for 2015.
sections.plainLanguage: Most drivers slow down when told to, but a few ignore the signs or drive faster to get ahead. Nobody has a perfect plan yet for those drivers, so the authors ask researchers to keep looking.

sections.title: The Seven Recommendations
sections.content:
Section 4 summarizes the guidance as seven recommendations. They are written with SHOULD because there may be unforeseen use cases, but the RFC warns that one should be careful in concluding that one's own case is an exception, since such cases have rarely, if ever, been observed and reported.

The core ones are that network devices SHOULD implement some AQM mechanism to manage queue lengths, reduce end-to-end latency and avoid lock-out, and that deployed AQM algorithms SHOULD support ECN as well as loss. Section 4.1 adds that when scheduling is used, AQM should be applied across the classes or flows as well as within each one.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors boil their advice down to seven short rules. Most of them say: warn early, warn the same way no matter who is sending, and do not make the person running the router twist knobs.

sections.title: Signaling Congestion with Drops and ECN
sections.content:
A device can signal congestion by delaying packets in a queue, dropping them, or marking them (for example with ECN). Added latency is an implicit signal; it affects TCP's ACK clocking, and methods like LEDBAT treat it as their primary congestion signal. The RFC calls the use of delay-based methods alongside AQM an area for further research.

Dropping protects the network and also tells reliable transports about incipient congestion, but it is an ambiguous signal, since loss can also mean faulty equipment or media, so a transport must conservatively assume congestion. The RFC calls congestion signaling by loss "a necessary evil". Network devices SHOULD use an AQM algorithm to measure local congestion and decide which packets to mark or drop, and AQM algorithms SHOULD randomize dropping in time so that congestion indications reach a wide share of the active flows rather than a few.

With ECN, a device sets the Congestion Experienced (CE) codepoint in the IP header, the receiver reports it back, and the sender reacts. Deciding when to set CE needs an AQM algorithm configured with a threshold. Devices SHOULD mark ECN-capable traffic when responding to congestion, and non-ECN-capable flows are dropped. Safe deployment also requires dropping excessive traffic even if it is marked as ECN-capable, because a receiver, sender or network device could hide or ignore an ECN mark. ECN support MAY have parameters separate from those for drop, which SHOULD still auto-tune and also be manually configurable.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can warn a sender by making packets wait, throwing some away, or sticking a "slow down" note on them. The note is friendlier than throwing things away, but the router must still throw things away if someone ignores the notes.

sections.title: Properties of a Good AQM Algorithm
sections.content:
The RFC sets out properties for AQM algorithms proposed for Internet deployment.

  • No operational tuning (4.3). Deployment SHOULD NOT require tuning, and an algorithm MUST provide a default behavior that auto-tunes to reasonable performance for typical conditions. Initial conditions such as interface rate and MTU MAY be required. Any manual variables SHOULD be externalized to the operator, and logging and alarm signals MAY be provided. Self-tuning algorithms are to be preferred.
  • Respond to measured congestion, not application profiles (4.4). An algorithm should not favor a packet size. When deciding to drop or mark, it is RECOMMENDED that the packet's size not be taken into account (see RFC 7141). An AQM system MAY run different algorithm instances within a traffic class, including separate ones for ECN-capable and non-ECN-capable packets.
  • Do not depend on specific transport behavior (4.5). AQM algorithms SHOULD NOT assume particular transports or applications. They should be shown to work beyond TCP, for example with UDP, SCTP and DCCP, and tunnels should be considered. Transports need to respond within a few RTTs at the latest.
  • Interactions with congestion control (4.6). Queued packets delay detection of congestion. A transport should try to operate below the knee of the load/delay curve. The correct operation of an AQM-enabled device MUST NOT rely upon specific transport responses to congestion signals.
sections.plainLanguage: A good early-warning system sets itself up, treats every kind of traffic by the same rules, and does not count on any one program behaving in a particular way.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says security is largely orthogonal to the performance issues it discusses. Because AQM must not depend on transport or application behavior, a device does not need to see upper-layer protocol information, which the RFC calls a privacy-enhancing feature. Section 6 states that the document by itself presents no new privacy issues.

Many deployed devices use queueing methods that let unresponsive traffic capture capacity from other flows, which could be exploited as a denial-of-service attack. AQM or scheduling can reduce that threat. However, an attack that produces unresponsive flows may be indistinguishable from legitimate traffic such as tunnels carrying aggregates of short flows, so new methods may remain vulnerable, and the RFC recommends that ongoing research consider mitigations.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the router does not need to peek inside what people are sending, it learns less about them. Bad actors who refuse to slow down can still be a problem, and people are still working on that.

items.label: Implement AQM
items.desc: Network devices SHOULD implement some AQM mechanism to manage queue lengths, reduce latency and avoid lock-out.

items.label: Support ECN
items.desc: Deployed AQM algorithms SHOULD support ECN as well as loss.

items.label: No tuning
items.desc: AQM algorithms SHOULD NOT require tuning of initial or configuration parameters in common use cases.

items.label: Measured congestion
items.desc: AQM algorithms SHOULD respond to measured congestion, not application profiles.

items.label: Transport-agnostic
items.desc: AQM algorithms SHOULD NOT interpret specific transport protocol behaviors.

items.label: Use capacity
items.desc: Congestion control algorithms SHOULD maximize use of available capacity without undue loss or round-trip delay.

items.label: Research
items.desc: Research, engineering and measurement are needed on flows that are unresponsive or more aggressive than TCP.
